tagline: Extending and testing the Kiraly and Tokai dictionary of the Rohonc Codex
intro:
The Rohonc Codex is a small paper book of the sixteenth century. It contains about 450 leaves and is kept at the Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in Budapest. It is written in a script that occurs in no other document. The writing runs right to left and uses several hundred signs.

Levente Zoltan Kiraly and Gabor Tokai established what the book contains. They published a dictionary of 841 signs and the grammar. Their work shows the codex contains the apocryphal Life of Adam and Eve running into the legend of the Rood, the story of Joachim and Anne, a Passion the codex itself says it takes from Matthew and John, sermons and parables for the gospels of the year, the Finding of the Cross, the Acts of the Apostles, and at the end a few pages of one man's diary. The frame is a revelation where an angel of God speaks and the prophet Elijah is the one addressed.

This project started from the Kiraly and Tokai dictionary. It tested their dictionary and extended it. It read signs their dictionary leaves undefined. It checked every reading at every place the sign stands in the book. It rendered the whole manuscript into English with every word marked by how well it is known.
how_far: The manuscript contains 29,997 words. This project reads 93.4% of them. Of all words in the manuscript, 3.2% are read from one passage only, 3.3% are restored in brackets, and 0.2% are dark. 81.6% of lines have every word read. Once brackets are counted, 98.9% of lines are complete.
tiers: The dictionary of added readings contains 1,787 entries. They are graded by how well they are known. Tier A readings survive every place the sign stands in the book, or are proved by an identical formula or a numeral. Tier B readings survive most places, with the rest unclear rather than against. Tiers C and D are read from one passage with nothing inside the book able to refuse them. Tier G is a guess, printed in brackets, and counted as read nowhere. 21 withdrawn readings stay in the file with the reason they went.

edition: The whole manuscript is being set as a book in two parts. It will contain a continuous retelling by episode and all 441 folios with their marked lines. It is being finished and will appear in the OONA Free Library. Nothing on this site waits on it.
credit: Levente Zoltan Kiraly and Gabor Tokai published the dictionary and transcription this project extends. Their own translation of the codex is unpublished. Roughly three quarters of the words this project reads are theirs or follow directly from theirs. The readings, tests, English and editorial matter on this site are this project's own.
reading_lead: This page presents one paragraph of English for each of the 441 folios, in Kiraly and Tokai's page order. Restorations are in brackets. The full per-word marks are in the edition and the rendering, not on this page.
dictionary_lead:
This dictionary contains the 1,787 readings this project added to the Kiraly and Tokai dictionary. Their own 841 entries are not reproduced here. The signs are written as glyph codes, using three hexadecimal digits per glyph. The drawn signs are on their site.

You can search by reading or by sign. You can filter by tier. Each entry shows the evidence line. The dictionary includes tier A, B, C, D, and G readings, and withdrawn entries with the reason they went.

card_script: Learn about the script itself and how it works.
script_intro:
The Rohonc Codex is written in a logographic script. A sign stands for a word or a whole phrase, not a sound. Kiraly and Tokai established this. Several hundred signs are in use. The writing runs right to left.

Where the signs came from is not settled. This project does not claim to know. The script occurs in no other document. A logographic script is not tied to any one language, since a sign meaning 'Lord' can be voiced in whatever the reader speaks. That is an argument from the structure of the script, not a tested result.
script_signs: The following control shows one sign's reading at a time.
script_numerals: Numerals are strokes that add, and a 'ten' written after a group multiplies that group by ten. This was checked four times. Ten-ten-ten-ten is forty at the forty days and forty nights. Two-two-ten is also forty at the forty days of rain. Six-two is eight at the circumcision on the eighth day. Six-six is twelve at the twelve apostles.
script_phrases: Phrases are written without a space. The example Kiraly and Tokai print is 'you-Mary', a single sign made of their sign for the second person pronoun joined to their sign for Mary. This project confirmed the construction independently.
script_shuffle_lead: Use the controls below to shuffle through the signs.
script_marks: In the rendering, a plain word is read. A word with * was read from one passage with nothing in the book able to refuse it. A word in [brackets] is a restoration and is counted as read nowhere. A hyphen inside a word means one sign read as the smaller signs it is built from. A ~ marks a spelling their own apparatus files as a variant.
script_plates: Twenty-six folios carry pictures, forty-nine pictures in all. The plates in this edition were redrawn by an image model from the library's low-resolution scan, because no print-quality scan is available. They are new drawings that follow the scribe's composition, not reproductions.
method_intro:
The method solves the problem of reading a sign the dictionary leaves undefined. It must be checkable. The check is that a reading must fit at every place the sign stands in the book, not just where it was found.

The method is a loop. It is written as standing orders. The bar for every test is declared before the test runs. A near miss is a miss. Failed attempts are kept and written up.
method_loop: The loop to read one unread sign has six numbered steps. They are listed after this paragraph.
method_bars: The bar for every test is written into the test's own file before it runs, and is never moved afterwards. A near miss is a miss. Failed attempts are kept and written up with the number they failed by.
method_mistakes: The following list names the mistakes that cost the most time.
method_code: Links to the programs themselves follow.
tests_intro:
The tests were designed to break the project's own readings. The reason the bar is declared first is so a near miss is a miss. The test fails if it does not meet the declared bar.

Nine tests were designed by the project. Then two outside reviewers were shown the write-up and asked what tests they would require. Those tests were run as specified.
tests_after: The passes and failures add up to a record of what the project could and could not prove.
sources_intro:
The manuscript is out of copyright. Kiraly and Tokai's dictionary, transcription and page images are theirs. They are credited on every page and linked, not rehosted.

The readings, tests, English and editorial matter are this project's own. Every figure on the site is read out of a saved run, never typed by hand.
docs_lead: The project's own working documents are described here. They are working files written for whoever runs the project next, not for a reader. They are kept accurate rather than tidy. Anyone who wants one can ask for it.
credit_line: This project rests on the dictionary of Kiraly and Tokai; their translation is unpublished, and the readings here are this project's own.
